t.1.160.1: Arjuna said: You addressed me here with the word "Tāpatya." I wish to know the precise meaning of that word "Tāpatya."
t.1.160.2: And who is this one named Tapatī, on whose account we are called Tāpatyas? For we are Kaunteyas, O good one; I wish to know the truth of this.
t.1.160.3: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the Gandharva narrated to Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, a tale renowned throughout the three worlds.
t.1.160.4: Well then, I shall tell you this delightful tale, righteous and complete, exactly as it happened, O Pārtha, best of the upholders of dharma.
t.1.160.5: The reason for which I addressed you with the word 'Tāpatya', that I shall tell you; listen to me with undivided mind.
t.1.160.6: He who here in the sky pervades the vault of heaven with his brilliance from his station, to him was born a daughter named Tapatī, without equal.
t.1.160.7: O son of Kuntī, O mighty one, Vivasvant had a daughter, Tapatī, the younger sister of Sāvitrī, renowned in the three worlds and endowed with austerity.
t.1.160.8: Neither goddess nor Asurī, neither Yakṣī nor Rākṣasī, neither Apsaras nor Gandharvī is there anywhere of such a form.
t.1.160.10: Savitṛ did not consider anyone in the three worlds, O Bhārata, a husband equal to her in beauty, character, lineage and learning.
t.1.160.9: Her faultless limbs were well proportioned, her eyes long and deep black; she was of good conduct and virtuous, finely attired, a radiant lady.
t.1.160.11: Seeing that his daughter had reached the bloom of youth and was ready to be given in marriage, he found no peace, as he kept pondering whom to give her to.
t.1.160.12: Now, O Kaunteya, the son of Ṛkṣa, the mighty bull among the Kurus, King Saṃvaraṇa, constantly worshipped Sūrya.
t.1.160.14: Eager to serve, free of self-conceit, and pure, the joy of the Pauravas, full of devotion, worshipped the rising radiant Sun.
t.1.160.13: Because the king constantly paid homage with offerings of arghya water and garlands, and with observances, fasts, and austerities of many kinds as well.
t.1.160.15: Then Sūrya deemed Saṃvaraṇa, grateful, knowing the dharma, and unequalled on earth in beauty, a fitting husband for Tapatī.
t.1.160.16: Then, O Kauravya, he wished to give that maiden to Saṃvaraṇa, the best of kings, whose lineage was renowned.
t.1.160.17: For just as the one of blazing rays, the sun, illumines the sky with his brilliance, so on earth did King Saṃvaraṇa shine with his radiance.
t.1.160.18: Just as the expounders of Brahman worship the rising sun, so, Pārtha, did the subjects born of orders lower than the brahmins worship Saṃvaraṇa.
t.1.160.19: In the eyes of friends and foes alike, that glorious king surpassed Soma in loveliness and Āditya in splendor.
t.1.160.21: Then once, O Pārtha, that glorious king, whose fame was wide upon the earth, went hunting, it is said, in a grove on the mountainside.
t.1.160.20: To that king, endowed with such virtues and of such conduct, O Kaurava, Tapana himself resolved to give Tapatī.
t.1.160.22: O Kaunteya, while that king was roaming on the mountain in pursuit of the hunt, his peerless horse, overcome by hunger, thirst and exhaustion, died.
t.1.160.23: That king, O Pārtha, his horse having died, wandering on foot upon the mountain, saw a long-eyed maiden who had no equal in the world.
t.1.160.24: Alone, coming upon that maiden who was alone, the crusher of foes, that tiger among kings, stood gazing at her with unwavering eyes.
t.1.160.25: For that king, judging by her beauty, took her to be Śrī herself; and then again he imagined her to be the radiance of the sun, as if fallen from it.
t.1.160.26: And the mountain plateau on which she, the lovely dark-eyed one, stood became, with its trees, shrubs and creepers, as though made of gold.
t.1.160.27: Having seen her, he thought little of the beauty of all other living beings, and the king considered that he had obtained the very fruit of his own eyes.
t.1.160.28: Of whatever forms that lord of the earth had seen since his birth, he could not conceive of any that was equal to hers.
t.1.160.29: His mind and eyes bound by her then with fetters woven of her charms, he did not stir from that place, nor was he aware of anything at all.
t.1.160.31: Thus then did King Saṃvaraṇa reflect upon the maiden, who was unequalled in the world in the wealth of her beauty.
t.1.160.30: Surely the Creator churned the whole world with its gods, asuras and men, and then brought forth and fashioned this beauty of this wide-eyed woman.
t.1.160.32: And as soon as he saw that lovely maiden, the king of noble lineage, tormented by the arrows of Kāma, fell to brooding in his mind.
t.1.160.33: Burning with the fierce fire of love, the king, bold himself, spoke to that glorious maiden, who was shy.
t.1.160.34: Who are you, and whose are you, O lady with thighs like plantain stems? For what purpose do you stand here? And how is it that you wander alone in this deserted forest, O sweetly smiling one?
t.1.160.35: For you, flawless in every limb and adorned with every ornament, are like the coveted adornment of these very ornaments.
t.1.160.37: Whatever beautiful women I have ever seen or even heard of, I do not consider any of them to be your equal, O proud and radiant lady.
t.1.160.36: I do not think you are a goddess, nor an Asura woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Rākṣasī, nor a serpent maiden, nor a Gandharvī, nor a human woman.
t.1.160.38: Thus did that protector of the earth speak to her, but she then answered nothing at all to him, tormented by desire as he was, in the lonely forest.
t.1.160.39: Then, while the king lamented again and again, the long-eyed maiden vanished right there, like lightning among the clouds.
t.1.160.40: Then, searching for her, the lotus-eyed maiden, the king roamed all about that forest, wandering like a madman.
t.1.160.41: But he, no longer seeing her, lamented much there, and that best of the Kauravas stood motionless for a moment.
